newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-SF Fed's Parry sees no new economic era.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-SF Fed's Parry sees no new economic era.

text.p: Robert Parry, the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, believes the U.S. economy has slowed in the second quarter from a torrid 5.8 percent expansion rate in the first three months of the year.
But still, he is skeptical.

He will cheer on the current exuberant state of the economy, the continued seven-year-old expansion with scant inflation and low unemployment. And he will also admit that he was somewhat surprised by some recent economic data, including a strong rise in consumer confidence in June.
But don't ask him to believe the economy has entered a "Brave New Era" where global competition will be enough to keep inflation down permanently.
"I think that there are a whole lot of positive things that one can point to in terms of inflation," Parry told Reuters in an interview here on Tuesday.

"But I don't that think we're in a new era where inflation is never going to be a concern. I think developments have been quite favorable, and somewhat surprisingly favorable, but I think basic laws of economics still apply."

Parry said that in a world of flexible foreign exchange rates, the argument that foreign countries may provide goods more cheaply and, therefore, put a permanent lid on U.S. inflation, is hard to sell.

That argument -- touted by some advocates of the so-called new global economy as the reason why U.S. inflation has remained low while unemployment is falling -- weakens even further when one takes into account that some 90 percent of all goods consumed in the U.S. are produced domestically.
"The relative importance of imports to our economy is much less than, say, if you were in Germany or in France or Italy or Great Britain," Parry said.
Also, the San Francisco Fed president added, that argument applies mostly to the manufacturing sector, which accounts roughly for one third of the U.S. economy.

It fails to take into consideration the increasing importance of the service sector. Thus, that argument is mostly irrelevant if you are talking about the price of a meal out or an Internet consultant fee, for example.

Parry said he believed the economy slowed to a more sustainable level in the second quarter of 1997, adding that he expected the U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would grow by around 2.0 percent in that period.

Parry refused to comment on whether the economy would continue to slow, but said his forecast for GDP growth for the period between the fourth quarter of 1996 and the fourth quarter of 1997 was around 3.0 percent.

"That 3.0 percent is very much influenced by the 5.8 percent (GDP growth) in the first quarter. If you get 5.8 percent in the first quarter and 2.0 percent in the second quarter, to get to 3.0 percent would require growth rates that are pretty sustainable," Parry said.
Parry has a seat in the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and, according to the committee's rotation rules, is scheduled to vote on monetary policy actions in 1997.

The FOMC meets next on July 1 and 2. The Fed last changed interest rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The central bank left interest rates unchanged at the May 20 meeting.
Parry, who refused to comment on the Fed's future monetary policy actions, also said there might have been increases in U.S. productivity, maybe even larger gains than the official statistics show.
But the San Francisco Fed chief added that the U.S. labor force has increased significantly, which has contributed to the low unemployment rate.
According to the latest statistics, the U.S. jobless rate was at 4.8 percent in May.
While the new-economy crowd believes that inflation is not a concern anymore and the concept of NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment) is no longer relevant, Parry is a not so sure.

The San Francisco Fed head said the consensus among economists appears to show that the NAIRU is currently somewhere between 5.5 and 5-3/4 percent, but added that he would not be surprised if that rate has fallen recently.

"I must admit it wouldn't surprise me if some people adjusted down their NAIRU. It is a little perplexing. It is not a fixed but a moving target at this point ... (but) I still keep the NAIRU in mind," he said.
Asked about the lag between the time when the unemployment rate drops below the perceived NAIRU and inflation begins to show its teeth, Parry said:
"The problem is that nowadays we haven't seen any (inflationary pressures), but one would have expected to see inflationary pressures built by now."

Parry also said he was "a little surprised" by the current levels of consumer confidence, which jumped to 129.6 in June against a revised 127.9 in May. The June numbers, released by the Conference Board on Tuesday, were the highest since the August 1969 reading of 131.7.

"In a way, it's a little surprising because we do have indications that consumer spending slowed rather significantly in the second quarter. So it's a little surprising to see a little pickup in consumer confidence," Parry said.

Parry said, however, he does not spend much time focusing on the index "because I think that consumer confidence is a reflection of the economy, not a very good predictor of what's going to happen to the economy (in the future)."
Among the economic indicators he will keep in mind going into the July FOMC meeting, Parry pointed to employment, industrial output and consumer spending data.
